parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: background radiation, detector geometry and absorption
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what each term means - activity is every disintegration in the whole sample, while count rate is only what this one small detector actually registers.
Hint 2: Think about direction - the sample in Fig. 13.1 radiates in all directions in 3D, but the detector only covers a small solid angle above it. What else could stop radiation reaching it?
Hint 3: Think about what could make the counter read too high as well as too low - extra sources of radiation and more than one detection per decay.
parts.proper_answer: Any three: background radiation is also counted; radiation is emitted in all directions so only a fraction reaches detector; some radiation is absorbed in sample, air, shielding or detector window; detector has dead-time and misses counts; one decay gives beta and gamma so may give >1 count; daughter product may also be radioactive.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Activity versus count rate**
Think of activity $A$ as the true physics - the number of copper-66 nuclei decaying per second in the whole sample, in $\text{Bq}$. Count rate is the engineering - the number of clicks per second your counter records. They are proportional but never equal.

Step 2: **Why the counter misses decays**
Decay radiation goes out in all directions, but the detector in Fig. 13.1 sits in one small position above. Most particles miss it completely. On the way, some $\beta^-$ particles are absorbed by self-absorption in the sample itself, by air, or by the detector window. Also after each ionisation the detector has a short dead-time when it cannot record another event.

Step 3: **Why the counter can over-read**
The counter also sees background radiation from cosmic rays, rocks and buildings. And here one copper-66 decay emits both a $\beta^-$ particle and a $\gamma$-ray photon, so one disintegration can produce two counts. If the daughter nucleus is also unstable it adds further activity.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Remember activity follows the same exponential fall as number of nuclei - a large drop from $3.62 \times 10^4$ to $1.21 \times 10^2$ in $42.0$ minutes means many half-lives have passed.
Hint 2: Write the decay law with half-life in the exponent, take natural logs of both sides, then isolate $T_{1/2}$ before putting numbers in your calculator.
parts.proper_answer: $$A = A_0 \exp(-\lambda t) = A_0 \exp(-\ln 2 \times t / T_{1/2})$$ $$1.21 \times 10^2 = 3.62 \times 10^4 \exp(-\ln 2 \times 42.0 / T_{1/2})$$ giving $T_{1/2} = 5.1 \text{ minutes}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the decay law**
Count rate is proportional to activity, so you can use count rates directly in the exponential law. With half-life $T_{1/2}$:
$$A = A_0 \exp\left(-\frac{\ln 2 \times t}{T_{1/2}}\right)$$
Here $A_0 = 3.62 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$, $A = 1.21 \times 10^2\text{ Bq}$ and $t = 42.0\text{ minutes}$.

Step 2: **Solve for half-life**
Divide and take natural logs:
$$\frac{1.21 \times 10^2}{3.62 \times 10^4} = \exp\left(-\frac{\ln 2 \times 42.0}{T_{1/2}}\right)$$
$$\ln\left(\frac{3.62 \times 10^4}{1.21 \times 10^2}\right) = \frac{\ln 2 \times 42.0}{T_{1/2}}$$
$$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2 \times 42.0}{\ln(299)} \approx 5.1\text{ minutes}$$

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Recall why atoms give sharp line spectra rather than continuous spectra - what does that tell you about electron energies, and what is the nuclear equivalent for sharp gamma energies?
parts.proper_answer: Nuclei, like atoms, have discrete / quantised energy levels. Gamma photons of specific energies correspond to transitions between these levels.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From lines to levels**
In atoms, sharp lines in an emission spectrum mean electrons jump between discrete energy levels, with photon energy $E = hf$ equal to the level difference. Seeing gamma photons with only specific, characteristic energies means exactly the same idea inside the nucleus - nuclei also have discrete, quantised energy levels and gamma emission is a transition between them.
